concept.name: Ex-dividend date
concept.definition: The first trading day on which a stock trades without the right to its declared dividend: buy on or after the ex-date and the seller, not you, receives the payment. It is set by stock-exchange rules, normally on the record date or one business day before if the record date is not a business day.
concept.intuition: Because trades take a day to settle, the ex-date is the practical cutoff: it answers 'how late can I buy and still get the dividend?'
concept.mechanics: Once a company sets the record date, the exchange fixes the ex-date so that only trades settling by the record date qualify, and the stock typically opens lower by about the dividend amount on the ex-date. For dividends of 25% or more of the stock's value, special rules defer the ex-date until one business day after payment.
concept.failure_modes: Dividend-capture strategies - buy before the ex-date, sell on it - fail in practice because the price drops by roughly the dividend and taxes on short-term trades erase any edge; large special dividends follow different ex-date rules that catch traders off guard.
concept.misconceptions: You do not need to own the stock on the record date itself - owning it before the ex-date so the trade settles in time is what counts, and selling on the ex-date still entitles you to the dividend.
concept.example: Investor.gov's example: declaration March 2, record date Monday March 16, ex-date March 16 - anyone buying on March 16 or later misses the March 17 payment.
